title: The questions everyone asks.
lead: Eight collapsible sections. Open any one to see the honest answer. If the question you have isn't here, ask us directly.

sections.title: License, repo, ship date, signed binaries

items.question: License, repo, ship date, signed binaries
items.answer_html:
License. Herald.OSS ships under Apache License 2.0. The LICENSE file lives at the repo root. Every Herald.Sinks.* package ships under Apache 2.0 too. Herald.Server and the Herald Dashboard are in Beta and will ship under Apache 2.0 at GA — the LICENSE lands with the GA release. Herald.Pro and Herald.Enterprise are commercial today, licensed per service; long-term source-availability terms are announced when those tiers exit Beta.

Contributing — CLA for Herald.OSS, DCO for Herald.Sinks. Two contribution paths. Herald.OSS uses a one-time Contributor License Agreement; Herald.Sinks uses Developer Certificate of Origin sign-off per commit.

ICLA / CCLA (Herald.OSS). Both flavours are adapted from the Apache Software Foundation's templates with substantive grants preserved verbatim:

  • ICLA (individuals, based on ASF ICLA v2.2) — signs once via the CLA bot using GitHub OAuth on Your first PR. Source at CLA/ICLA.md in the Herald.OSS repo.
  • CCLA (corporations, based on ASF CCLA v2.0) — authorised signer emails a signed PDF to legal@mmpworks.com; Schedule A lists employees designated to contribute. Source at CLA/CCLA.md.

DCO (Herald.Sinks). Every commit in Your pull request carries a Signed-off-by: trailer (added by git commit -s). A GitHub Action fails the build if any commit lacks the sign-off or the sign-off email doesn't match the commit author. No external signature store, no one-time enrollment — sign-off rides on every commit.

Why a CLA exists for the kernel but not the sinks: the sublicense right in §2 of both CLA templates is what lets MMPWorks redistribute kernel contributions under any future license terms (including the paid Pro/Enterprise tiers) without needing to chase every contributor for a re-sign. Sinks ship under permissive Apache 2.0 with no relicense agenda, so DCO is the right weight there.

Repo. github.com/mmpworks/Herald.OSS. Source, tests, benchmarks, soak harness, build scripts — everything that produced the numbers on this site.

NuGet. dotnet add package Herald.OSS. Multi-target for net8.0 / net9.0 / net10.0. AOT-clean public surface.

Available. Herald.OSS 1.0.0 on NuGet 2026-05-18. Subsequent point releases follow the standard SemVer cadence.

Signed binaries. Pro and Enterprise distributions are strong-named (PublicSign on for Apache 2.0 Herald.OSS; full Authenticode signing on the commercial tiers). Public key fingerprint is published in the repo's SECURITY.md.

sections.title: Migration from Serilog / NLog / log4net / MEL

items.question: Migration from Serilog / NLog / log4net / MEL
items.answer_html:
Serilog. One-line builder swap on the host side; existing ILogger<T> call sites stay unchanged via the MEL provider:

// Program.cs
builder.Logging.AddHeraldLogging(opts => opts
    .WithMinimumLevel("info")
    .WithConsoleSink());

Typical migration cost: 1–2 days per service if you stay on the MEL bridge; another 1–3 days if you switch high-volume call sites to Herald typed-args for the zero-allocation accept path.

NLog. Replace NLog.LogManager.GetCurrentClassLogger() with HeraldRegistry.GetLogger<T>(). NLog targets map 1:1 to Herald sinks; the typed-args call shape is identical. Concretely:

// NLog before
private static readonly NLog.Logger _log = NLog.LogManager.GetCurrentClassLogger();
_log.Info("User {Id} signed in", userId);

// Herald after
private static readonly ILogger _log = HeraldRegistry.GetLogger<MyService>();
_log.Info("User {Id} signed in", userId);

NLog config files (nlog.config) are not directly compatible — Herald uses fluent QuickLogBuilder at host startup or JSON config via HeraldRegistry.LoadFromJson(). The herald migrate CLI tool reads an nlog.config and emits the equivalent Herald JSON config. Typical NLog → Herald migration: 2–3 days per service including config translation.

log4net. log4net's appender model has the loosest mapping — two paths depending on how your codebase uses it:

  • If you use log4net through MEL (modern ASP.NET Core hosts via ILogger<T>): swap providers; call sites unchanged. Same as Serilog above.
  • If you use log4net directly (LogManager.GetLogger(...) + InfoFormat): replace with HeraldRegistry.GetLogger<T>() + typed args. InfoFormat(template, arg0, arg1) becomes Info(template, arg0, arg1). Appenders map to Herald sinks via the herald migrate --from-log4net-config tool that reads log4net.config XML and emits Herald JSON.

Typical log4net → Herald migration: 3–5 days per service. The longest part is replacing call sites; the appender-to-sink mapping is mechanical.

MEL. Already using ILogger<T>? Add Herald as a provider. Zero call-site changes. Pick up the zero-allocation accept path by switching LogInformation to the Herald typed-args overloads at hot sites.

items.question: AOT + trim-publish behavior
items.answer_html:
Herald.Core sets <IsAotCompatible>true</IsAotCompatible> and ships with EnableAotAnalyzer + EnableTrimAnalyzer on. Every JSON path on the public surface routes through a source-generated JsonSerializerContext — no reflection-based serialisation.

The source generator TypedArgsOverloadGenerator emits annotation-free call sites (no [RequiresUnreferencedCode] at the public boundary), so consumer PublishAot builds compile without warnings on the Herald-attributable surface.

The Apache Core CI runs PublishAot=true on every commit and asserts the resulting single-file binary boots and emits one event — if a PR regresses AOT cleanliness it fails before merge. Pro and Enterprise loggers are AOT-compatible too; no reflection paths in the resilience or audit code.

sections.title: Production status, design partners, GA milestones

items.question: Production status, design partners, GA milestones
items.answer_html:
Herald.Core 1.0.0 is available 2026-05-18 under Apache 2.0. The kernel and its tests have been validated extensively against the published benchmark harness and 6-hour soak before release, but Herald ships without pre-1.0 design partners — no paid pilots, no NDA references, no production testimonials yet.

Pro reliability decorators are GA. The HMAC-chain Enterprise audit decorator is GA with a 90-day post-release window during which the chain canonicalisation format is locked under a stability promise.

The case for trusting the product rests on what you can verify yourself: the benchmark harness, soak harness, and competitive bench are all in the public repo. Run them. If your own measurements land where ours did, you have your own data point — not someone else's reference story.

sections.title: Support SLA, security disclosure, who we are

items.question: Support SLA, security disclosure, who we are
items.answer_html:
Company. MMPWorks LLC. Steve Muchow is the technical lead. Engineering and support are MMPWorks-employed, not contracted.

Support SLAs.

  • Community — GitHub Issues, best-effort, no SLA.
  • Pro — business-hours response, 24-hour acknowledgement on critical issues.
  • Enterprise — 4-hour sev-1 response, 24×7 critical coverage, named support contact.

Security disclosure. 90-day coordinated disclosure window. Report vulnerabilities to security@mmpworks.com; PGP key in the repo SECURITY.md. Public advisories ship as GitHub Security Advisories with CVE assignment where applicable.

Signed binaries. Pro and Enterprise NuGet packages are Authenticode-signed by MMPWorks LLC. Apache Core packages carry strong-name signatures (PublicSign on); the key fingerprint is published in SECURITY.md so consumers can verify provenance.

sections.title: The "$0" claim — what it covers, what it doesn't

items.question: The "$0" claim — what it covers, what it doesn't
items.answer_html:
The strikethrough → $0 cards on the home page refer to the GC-waste line item only — the bytes per call your current logger allocates onto the managed heap, the CPU cycles the .NET garbage collector then has to spend cleaning them up, and the memory-tier overhead from a working set that sustains those allocations. Herald's zero-allocation accept path eliminates that line item.

You still pay your cloud provider for: sink egress (Datadog/Splunk/CloudWatch ingest), log storage, the CPU your service's actual work consumes, and the infrastructure your application runs on. Herald doesn't change any of that — it removes the allocator tax that logging would otherwise stack on top.

The "2.5 TB/day per service" figure is a measured value: at 40 kHz / service sustained, 720 B per Serilog call × 86400 seconds = 2.49 TB/day of allocation pressure the GC has to manage. Herald produces 0 B on the same workload — confirmed by the 6-hour soak (zero Gen0/Gen1/Gen2 collections across the run).

The dollar figures ($6K / $60K / $601K) are the conservative model: 40 kHz/service, 7% GC-overhead share of CPU, 1.5 GB memory-tier delta per service, $0.05/vCPU-hour, $5/GB-month. Every assumption is in the Competitors page cost matrix and can be substituted with your own cloud rates.
